board_events.text: When is a collection a SET?
A set is a well-defined collection: for any object you can answer 'in or out?' with a definite yes/no.
The objects inside are its elements (members).
'Tall students' is NOT a set. 'Students taller than 170 cm' IS.
Membership: $a \in A$ (a is in A), $b \notin A$ (b is not in A).
Repetition & order irrelevant: {1, 2, 2, 3} = {1, 2, 3}, {a, b, c} = {c, a, b}.
So 'how many elements?' always means how many DISTINCT elements.
Empty set $\emptyset$ = { }: no members at all.
Two languages for one set
Roster (tabular) form: list every member inside braces, e.g. {2, 4, 6}.
Set-builder form: state the rule members satisfy, $A = \{x : P(x)\}$.
The colon ':' reads 'such that'.
Roster is concrete but useless for endless collections; set-builder captures infinite sets in one line.
Roster can only hint at infinity with dots: {1, 2, 3, ...} — never truly list it.
Roster lists every 'yes'. Set-builder writes the yes/no question itself.
Classifying sets & comparing them
{0} is NOT empty (one element: 0). {∅} is NOT empty (one element: ∅).
Singleton: exactly one element, e.g. {a}.
Finite: $n(A)$ is a definite whole number. Infinite: not finite.
Equal sets $A = B$: identical elements (mutual containment).
Equivalent sets: same cardinality, $n(A) = n(B)$.
Equal ⇒ equivalent, but equivalent ⇏ equal. {1,2,3} & {a,b,c}: equivalent, not equal.
The universes you'll meet everywhere
$\mathbb{N} = \{1,2,3,\dots\}$ naturals; $\mathbb{W} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$ wholes.
$\mathbb{Z} = \{\dots,-2,-1,0,1,2,\dots\}$ integers; $\mathbb{Q} = \{p/q : p,q \in \mathbb{Z},\ q \ne 0\}$ rationals.
$\mathbb{R}$ = reals; irrationals $\mathbb{T}$ = reals that are not rational.

segments.text: <curious> Let's start with the one question this whole chapter rests on. When does a collection of things actually count as a set?

A set is any well defined collection. Well defined means this: pick any object in the universe, and you can say 'in' or 'out' with a definite yes or no. Picture a cricket captain's team sheet. Either your name is on the eleven, or it isn't. There's no debate.
The objects sitting inside the set are called its elements, or members.

Here's the catch that trips people. The set of tall students is not a set, because tall is just an opinion. But the set of students taller than one hundred seventy centimetres is a genuine set. Measure anyone and you get a clean yes or no.
We write a belongs to A using the epsilon like symbol, and b does not belong to A using that same symbol struck through.

Two rules fall straight out of the team sheet. Repetition means nothing, writing a name twice doesn't field two players, so the set one, two, two, three is just one, two, three. And order means nothing, reshuffling the line up changes nobody, so a, b, c equals c, a, b.
Because of that, whenever we ask how many elements, we always mean how many distinct elements.

And one special set deserves respect: the empty set, written with the slashed symbol or empty braces. It has no members at all, like the set of students who scored above one hundred on a one hundred mark paper. Nobody qualifies.
Once you have a set, how do you describe it to someone else? There are exactly two languages, and this section is about switching fluently between them.
The first is roster form, also called tabular form. You simply read out every member by name inside braces. The set of even numbers up to six is two, four, six. It's like reading a team sheet aloud.
The second is set builder form. Instead of naming members, you state the rule they all satisfy. In symbols, A equals the set of all x such that P of x holds, where P is the defining property.
That colon in the middle is important, it reads as 'such that'. So A equals x such that x is even, is just 'the set of all x such that x is even'.
Why keep both? Roster is concrete but hopeless for huge or endless collections, you cannot list every natural number. Set builder is a single rule that captures even an infinite set in one line.
Roster can only suggest an infinite set with dots, one, two, three, and so on. Those dots are a hint, they never truly list the set.
Here's the clean way to hold the difference. Roster form lists every 'yes'. Set builder form writes down the yes or no question itself.
Now let's give sets their labels, and learn the two ways to compare them. This is where a lot of easy marks are quietly won or lost.

First, the trap everyone falls into. The set containing zero is not the empty set, it holds one element, the number zero. Likewise the set containing the empty set is not empty, it holds one element, namely the empty set itself. A box with an empty box inside is still not an empty box.
A set with exactly one element is called a singleton, like the set containing just a.
A set is finite if its number of elements, written n of A, is a definite whole number you could finish counting. If you can never finish counting, it's infinite.
Now comparing. Two sets are equal, A equals B, when they have identical elements, every element of A is in B and every element of B is in A.
Two sets are merely equivalent when they only have the same cardinality, that is, n of A equals n of B, the same head count.

<whisper> Here's the exam secret. Equal always implies equivalent, but equivalent does not imply equal. The set one, two, three and the set a, b, c are equivalent, both have size three, yet they are absolutely not equal. Same count is not same faces.
In set builder form you always work inside some universe of numbers, so let's memorise the standard ones. These are the most common universes you'll see for the rest of your maths.
The naturals, capital N, are one, two, three, and onward. Add zero and you get the wholes, capital W, zero, one, two, and onward.

Bring in the negatives and you get the integers, capital Z, running from minus infinity through zero to plus infinity. Allow ratios p over q with integer p and q, and q not zero, and you get the rationals, capital Q.
The reals, capital R, are the full number line. And the irrationals, capital T, are exactly the reals that are not rational, numbers like root two and pi.
The key relationship is this chain of nesting: the naturals sit inside the wholes, inside the integers, inside the rationals, inside the reals. Each is a subset of the next.

Picture it as concentric ovals. Naturals in the centre, then integers, then rationals, then reals as the outer boundary. The shaded band, the part of the reals lying outside the rationals, is the irrationals, where root two and pi live.

Burn this in: the universe symbol quietly decides the answer. The set of x with x squared equals two is empty over the naturals, but a two element set over the reals. Always read the universe before you solve.

board_events.text: Two-digit numbers, digits adding to 8
Want: two-digit numbers (10–99) with digit-sum = 8. Let tens digit $t \ge 1$, units $u$, with $t + u = 8$.
80 qualifies: 8 + 0 = 8. Don't drop it!
Spot the empty set — fast
Options:
(b) {x : x is an even prime}
(d) $\{x \in \mathbb{N} : x < 1\}$
(a) $x^2 = -1$ has no real solution → EMPTY.
(d) smallest natural is 1, so no natural is $< 1$ → EMPTY.
(b) = {2}, NOT empty (2 is prime). (c) = {0}, NOT empty. Both are decoys.
Speed move: check the universe FIRST — ℕ starting at 1 kills (d) instantly.
Find n(A), n(B); is A = B?
$A = \{x \in \mathbb{Z} : |x| \le 2\}$,  $B = \{x \in \mathbb{Z} : x^3 = x\}$.
Every element of B is in A, but −2, 2 ∈ A are not in B → A ≠ B (in fact B ⊂ A).
For which a is n(T) = 1?
$T = \{x \in \mathbb{N} : x^2 - (a+1)x + a = 0\}$, $a$ a real parameter.

board_events.latex: x^2 - (a+1)x + a = (x-1)(x-a) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; x = 1 \text{ or } x = a

board_events.text: Root $x = 1 \in \mathbb{N}$ always. The root $x = a$ counts only if $a \in \mathbb{N}$, and is distinct only if $a \ne 1$.
If $a \in \mathbb{N},\ a \ne 1$: $T = \{1, a\}$, $n(T) = 2$.
If $a = 1$: roots coincide, $T = \{1\}$. If $a \notin \mathbb{N}$: only 1 survives, $T = \{1\}$.
n(T) = 1 ⟺ a = 1 OR a ∉ ℕ (i.e. a is not a natural number greater than 1).
Traps that quietly cost marks
Treating {0} or {∅} as empty. Both are singletons; empty means ZERO elements.
Counting repeats: 'MATHEMATICS' has 11 letters but only 8 distinct.
Ignoring the universe: {x : x² = 2} is empty over ℕ, a doubleton over ℝ.
Confusing equal with equivalent: same count ≠ same elements.
PRO-TIP: circle the universe symbol first and ask 'is this even possible here?'

segments.text: Our first worked example is a classic board question: write, in roster form, the set of all two digit natural numbers whose digits add up to eight.

Set up the structure. A two digit number lives between ten and ninety nine. Call the tens digit t and the units digit u. Since it's a two digit number, t is at least one, and the condition is t plus u equals eight. Now just walk t upward.

t equals one gives u equals seven, the number seventeen. t equals two, u equals six, gives twenty six. t equals three, u equals five, gives thirty five. t equals four, u equals four, gives forty four.
Keep going. t equals five gives fifty three, t equals six gives sixty two, t equals seven gives seventy one, and t equals eight gives eighty.
Watch this last one carefully, it's where marks vanish. Eighty qualifies, because eight plus zero equals eight. Students routinely drop it because the units digit is zero. Don't.
So the answer, in roster form, is seventeen, twenty six, thirty five, forty four, fifty three, sixty two, seventy one, eighty. Eight numbers, listed cleanly in braces.
Here's a speed trap, the kind where the exam rewards recognition over calculation. Without lengthy work, identify which of four options is the empty set.
The options are: a, the reals x with x squared plus one equals zero; b, x that is an even prime; c, the set containing zero; and d, natural numbers x less than one.
Scan for impossibility. Option a says x squared equals minus one, which has no real solution, so over the reals it is empty.
Option d, the smallest natural number is one, so no natural number is strictly less than one. Empty again.

Now the decoys. Option b is the set containing two, because two is the one and only even prime, so it's not empty, students forget two is prime. And option c contains the number zero, so it's not empty either, that's the classic set containing zero versus empty set trap.
The real lesson is the speed move: check the universe before you compute. In option d, seeing that the naturals start at one instantly kills it, no arithmetic needed. Domain first, always.
This one links absolute value reasoning with polynomial factoring, over a restricted universe. We need the size of two sets, and whether they're equal.
A is the integers x with absolute value of x at most two. B is the integers x satisfying x cubed equals x. Note both live in the integers, that restriction matters.
For A, absolute value at most two means x runs from minus two to two: minus two, minus one, zero, one, two. So n of A is five.
For B, rearrange x cubed equals x to x cubed minus x equals zero, then factor: x times x minus one times x plus one equals zero. The roots are minus one, zero, and one, all integers.
So B is minus one, zero, one, and n of B is three.

Now test equality with mutual containment. Every element of B does lie in A, good, but minus two and two are in A and not in B. Containment fails one direction, so A is not equal to B. In fact B is a proper subset of A. Final answer: n of A is five, n of B is three, and A is not equal to B.

This is an Advanced level problem, and the whole thing turns on remembering the domain. The set T lives in the naturals, and we want to find every value of the parameter a for which T has exactly one element.
T is the natural numbers x satisfying x squared minus a plus one, times x, plus a, equals zero. Here a is any real number, that's the parameter we're solving for.

First factor the quadratic, which is independent of the domain. x squared minus a plus one x plus a factors beautifully as x minus one, times x minus a. So the two roots are x equals one, and x equals a.

board_events.text: When is one set inside another?
$A \subseteq B$: every element of A is also an element of B (B may have extras).
Always: $A \subseteq A$ (self) and $\emptyset \subseteq B$ (empty is a subset of every set).
Proper subset $A \subsetneq B$: $A \subseteq B$ AND $A \ne B$ (B has at least one extra).
Superset: $B \supseteq A$ means B contains A.

board_events.latex: A = B \iff (A \subseteq B \text{ and } B \subseteq A)

board_events.text: Element-to-set vs set-to-set
∈ relates an element to a set; ⊆ relates a set to a set. Never mix them.
e.g. $1 \in \{1,2\}$ (element), but $\{1\} \subseteq \{1,2\}$ (subset). Writing $1 \subseteq A$ is a category error.
Universal set $U$: all objects under discussion. Every set here is a subset of $U$.
Interval = an unbroken stretch of ℝ. $<$ → round bracket (open); $\le$ → square bracket (closed).

segments.text: <curious> When do we say one set sits inside another? Picture the fifteen member squad India announces, and the playing eleven the captain picks from it.

Every player in the eleven is also in the squad, and that is exactly the idea of a subset. A is a subset of B, written A with the cup shaped symbol under it pointing at B, when every element of A is also an element of B. Crucially, B is allowed extras, the bench players, all we demand is that nobody in A is missing from B.

Two boundary cases always hold, and both trip students up. Every set is a subset of itself, the full squad is a valid selection from the full squad. And the empty set is a subset of every set, the empty guest list breaks no rule of any party, because to fail you'd need to point at someone on it who wasn't invited, and there's nobody to point at.
When A is a subset of B but not the whole of B, so there's at least one extra in B, we call A a proper subset, written with the cup symbol carrying a slash, or a strict subset sign.
And then B is called a superset of A, written with the symbol flipped the other way. The playing eleven is a proper subset of the squad, the squad is a superset of the eleven.
Finally, the cleanest test for equality: A equals B exactly when A is a subset of B and B is a subset of A. Mutual containment both ways is equality.
This section holds the single most important hurdle in the whole chapter: the difference between the two symbols, belongs to, and is a subset of.
The belongs to symbol relates an element to a set. The subset symbol relates a set to a set. They live at different levels, and mixing them is the most common error you'll make if you're not careful.

Concretely, one belongs to the set one, two, because one is an element. But the set containing one is a subset of the set one, two. Writing one is a subset of A, or the set containing one belongs to A, is a category error. A player is in the team, a partnership is part of the team.

Now widen the lens. Every discussion happens inside some agreed playing field, the set of all objects currently under consideration. That's the universal set, capital U. In an election it's all registered voters, in a number chapter it might be the integers or the reals. Every set in the discussion is a subset of U.

A special continuous case of subset of the reals is an interval, an unbroken stretch of the number line. Read the inequality type: a strict less than becomes a round bracket, meaning the endpoint is excluded, open. A less than or equal becomes a square bracket, meaning the endpoint is included, closed.

Look at the picture. The interval two, five, written square bracket two comma five round bracket, includes two, the filled dot, and excludes five, the open dot. The square bracket is a promise that the endpoint belongs.

And a warning that surprises people: an interval like open two to five is an infinite set. It looks small on the page, but between any two reals there are infinitely many more. Small width does not mean few elements.

segments.text: Now meet the power set, the object behind almost every counting question in this subtopic.
Take a small set, a and b. List all its possible sub selections: the empty set, the set with just a, the set with just b, and the set with both. Four of them.
The set whose members are all these subsets is called the power set of A, written P of A, formally the set of all X such that X is a subset of A.
So the power set is the complete menu of every sub selection you could possibly make from A. Its members are themselves sets, that's the key mental shift.

Here's the engine that powers everything. To build a subset of A, walk down the list of elements and, for each one, flip a coin, in or out. With n elements you make n independent two way choices, so you get two times two times two, n times, which is two to the power n subsets.

And notice the belongs to versus subset distinction returning, sharper now. The set containing one is a subset of one, two, but the same set containing one is an element, a member, of the power set of one, two. Same object, different relationship, depending on which set you compare it to.
Let's lay out the counting toolkit for a set with n elements. These formulas turn a whole family of exam questions into one line of arithmetic.
The headline: the number of subsets, that is the size of the power set, is two to the power n. This is the one to memorise cold.

From it, the number of proper subsets is two to the n minus one, since we exclude only the full set itself. And the number of non empty subsets is also two to the n minus one, since we exclude only the empty set. Different reason, same number.
The number of non empty proper subsets is two to the n minus two, excluding both extremes. And the number of subsets with exactly r elements is n choose r, the binomial coefficient.

Now the derivation, so this is understanding, not memorising. To specify a subset, you decide for each element, independently, whether it's in or out. That's two choices for the first element, times two for the second, and so on.

So the total is two multiplied by itself n times, which is two to the power n. The all out choice gives the empty set, the all in choice gives the full set, so this count already includes both improper subsets, which is exactly why proper subsets are one fewer.

And here's a beautiful cross check using the binomial theorem. Subsets of size zero, plus size one, all the way to size n, is n choose zero plus n choose one, up to n choose n, which equals one plus one, all to the power n, which is two to the n. The two routes agree perfectly.
Let's build a power set carefully, and use the trick that guarantees you never miss a subset: list by size, smallest first.
Start at size zero, that's the empty set, one of them. Then size one, the singletons: the set p, the set q, the set r, three of them. Starting from the empty set is what stops people forgetting it.
Next, size two, the pairs: p q, p r, and q r, three of them. And finally size three, the full set p q r, one of them.
So the power set of A is the collection of all eight: the empty set, the three singletons, the three pairs, and the full set. Notice every member here is itself a set.
And the count checks out: n of the power set is two to the power three, which is eight, exactly what we listed. If your list doesn't hit the power of two, you've missed something.

The picture shows this as a power set lattice. The empty set sits at the bottom, the full set p q r at the top, and each subset connects upward to the subsets one element larger. Organising by size is what prevents the two commonest omissions, forgetting the empty set and forgetting the full set.

board_events.text: Given n[P(A)] = 256
Speed move: recognise the power of two. $256 = 2^8$.
Trap A: n(A) = 256 is wrong — 256 is the number of subsets, not elements.
Trap B: proper = 254 is wrong — subtract 1 (only the set itself is excluded), not 2.
Find n[P(A)] for a quadratic-defined A
$A = \{x \in \mathbb{Z} : x^2 - x - 6 \le 0\}$.
The integer domain is decisive: over ℝ, A = [−2, 3] is infinite — no finite power-set count.
A = {1,2,3,4,5,6,7}: two subset counts
(a) 'Only odd numbers' = a subset of O.
(b) 'At least one even' = (all subsets) − (subsets with no even).
Where subset/power-set marks vanish
∈ vs ⊆: $1 \in A$, but $\{1\} \subseteq A$ and $\{1\} \in P(A)$.
Forgetting ∅ and A itself when listing subsets. Organise by size so you can't miss them.
Proper subsets = $2^n - 1$ (exclude only A), NOT $2^n - 2$.
Reading $n[P(A)]$ as $n(A)$: if $n[P(A)] = 1024 = 2^{10}$, then $n(A) = 10$, never 1024.
PRO-TIP: memorise 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024 — half of power-set MCQs are just 'spot the power of two'.

segments.text: A pure speed trap. You're told the power set of A has two hundred fifty six members, and asked for the number of elements in A and the number of proper subsets.

The move that saves you is instant recognition of a power of two. Two hundred fifty six is two to the power eight. Memorising the small powers of two turns this from a sixty second problem into a five second one.
Now, the size of the power set is two to the power n of A, and we're told that equals two to the eight. So n of A is simply eight.
The number of proper subsets is two to the eight minus one, which is two hundred fifty five, since we exclude only the full set itself.

Now the two traps. Trap A, writing n of A equals two hundred fifty six. But two hundred fifty six is the number of subsets, not the number of elements. Don't confuse the power set's size with the set's size.

Trap B, writing two hundred fifty four for proper subsets by wrongly subtracting two. Only the set itself is excluded from being proper, so you subtract one, giving two hundred fifty five. The off by one here is a classic examiner trap.
This one stitches together three skills: a quadratic inequality, an integer domain, and the power set count. Watch how the domain quietly controls the answer.
A is the integers x satisfying x squared minus x minus six, less than or equal to zero. So first we solve the inequality, then we filter to integers.

Factor the quadratic: x squared minus x minus six is x minus three, times x plus two. A product of two factors is less than or equal to zero exactly between its roots, so x runs from minus two to three.
Now the domain kicks in. Over the integers, x from minus two to three means minus two, minus one, zero, one, two, three. That's six integers, so n of A is six.
The power set count is then two to the power six, which is sixty four. Clean.

And here's the lesson worth underlining. The integer domain is decisive. If instead the universe were the reals, A would be the entire closed interval from minus two to three, an infinite set, with no finite power set count at all. Same inequality, completely different answer, purely because of the domain.
An Advanced favourite. Take the set one through seven, and answer two counting questions, the second of which teaches the reflex that separates strong students.
First, split the set. The odd numbers are one, three, five, seven, that's four of them. The even numbers are two, four, six, that's three of them.
Part a asks for subsets containing only odd numbers. A subset made purely of odd numbers is precisely a subset of the odd set. So we just count subsets of a four element set.
By the coin flip argument, that's two to the power four, which is sixteen. And note, this count includes the empty set, which technically has no even numbers, so it correctly counts as odd only.

Part b asks for subsets with at least one even number. Here's the reflex, don't sum exactly one even, exactly two evens, and so on. Instead use the complement principle: at least one even equals all subsets, minus the subsets with no even number at all.

Subsets with no even number are exactly the subsets of the odd set, which is sixteen. Total subsets of the whole seven element set are two to the seven, which is one hundred twenty eight. So the answer is one hundred twenty eight minus sixteen, which is one hundred twelve. Counting the easy opposite and subtracting is the standard Advanced move.
Let's gather the traps that quietly drain marks in subsets and power sets, so they never catch you.

Trap one, and the biggest, confusing belongs to with subset. Elements join a set with belongs to, sub collections relate with subset. One belongs to A, but the set containing one is a subset of A, and that same set containing one is an element of the power set of A. Three true statements, three different symbols.
Trap two, forgetting the empty set and the full set itself when listing subsets. They are always there, both of them. Organise by size, smallest first, and you literally cannot miss them.
Trap three, the off by one in proper subsets. Proper subsets is two to the n minus one, you exclude only the set itself, not two to the n minus two. Subtracting two is a reflex error, resist it.

Trap four, reading the size of the power set as the size of the set. If the power set has one thousand twenty four members, that's two to the ten, so the set has ten elements, never one thousand twenty four.

And the pro tip that pays off constantly: memorise the small powers of two, two, four, eight, sixteen, thirty two, sixty four, one twenty eight, two fifty six, five twelve, one thousand twenty four. Half of all power set multiple choice questions reduce to spotting which power of two you're looking at, and instant recognition turns a minute long problem into a five second one.

board_events.text: Five ways to ask 'who's in?'
Union $A \cup B$: in A OR B (inclusive 'or' — both counts).
Intersection $A \cap B$: in BOTH. Keyword 'and'.
Difference $A - B$: in A but NOT in B. One-directional: $A - B \ne B - A$.
Complement $A'$: everyone in U not in A. Meaningless until U is fixed.
Symmetric difference $A \triangle B = (A-B) \cup (B-A)$: in exactly one, never both.
Disjoint: $A \cap B = \emptyset$ — the two sets share nobody.
Turn bookkeeping into a picture
Draw U as a rectangle, each set as a circle. Two overlapping circles carve 4 regions.

segments.text: <curious> Think of two broadcast lists on your phone, Family and Office, and all your contacts together as the universe. Every set operation is just a way of asking a membership question about these two lists.

First, union, A cup B. That's everyone in Family or Office, or both. If you're sending a wedding invite to both circles, you message the union. Burn in the word 'or', and it's the inclusive or, both counts.
Second, intersection, A cap B. That's everyone in both lists, like a cousin who's also a colleague. The keyword here is 'and'.

Third, difference, A minus B. Those in Family but not in Office. Notice this is one directional, B minus A, in Office but not Family, is a completely different group. Set subtraction, like number subtraction, is not commutative.

Fourth, complement, A prime. Everyone in your contacts who is not in Family. Complement always means 'everyone else', so it only makes sense once you've fixed the universe U. Change U and the complement changes with it.
Fifth, symmetric difference, A triangle B. Those in exactly one of the two lists, never both, the people who attended only one of two functions. Formally it's A minus B, unioned with B minus A.
And when two lists share nobody at all, say Family and total Strangers, we call them disjoint, meaning their intersection is the empty set.
The reason Venn diagrams are so powerful is that they turn all this membership bookkeeping into a single picture you can just read.
Draw the universe as a rectangle, and each set as a circle inside it. Two overlapping circles carve the rectangle into exactly four regions, and every element of U lands in exactly one of them.

Look at the four regions in the picture: only A, the left crescent, only B, the right crescent, the lens in the middle which is A intersect B, and the outside corner, neither, which is everything in neither circle.
Here's the liberating idea. Once you see those four regions, every operation is simply a choice of which regions to shade.
Union shades three regions, everything except neither. Intersection shades only the lens, the overlap.
A minus B shades only the 'only A' crescent. And A prime, the complement, shades everything outside circle A, both the 'only B' crescent and the neither corner.
So the payoff is real: you never have to memorise the operations as rules. You just decide which regions the words describe, and shade them.
The Venn picture makes one of the most useful rules in the chapter obvious, De Morgan's laws, which tell you what happens when you complement a whole combination.
Ask, what does 'not in Family or Office' mean? It means you're outside both circles, which is the same as saying not in Family and not in Office. The 'or' inside became an 'and' outside.
In symbols, the complement of A union B equals A prime intersect B prime. Flipping a union then complement turns the or into an and.
The twin law: the complement of A intersect B equals A prime union B prime. Same idea running the other way.

You can prove this by element chasing. Track an arbitrary x. x is outside A union B exactly when x is not in A and not in B. Every step is a logical if and only if, so the two sides have exactly the same elements. The negation of 'or' being 'and' is the entire law.
Hold the one liner: complement a union, you get an intersection. Complement an intersection, you get a union. The operation flips, every time.
And a clean division of labour: shading a Venn diagram illustrates De Morgan, but the element chase is what actually proves it.
Set algebra is a genuine algebra: treat union like plus, intersection like times, and complement like negation. Here is the toolkit, board shows each law, and I'll say it in words.
Commutative and associative: A union B equals B union A, and grouping doesn't matter, A union B, then union C, equals A union the quantity B union C. The same holds for intersection.
Distributive: A intersect the quantity B union C equals A intersect B, unioned with A intersect C. Intersection distributes over union just like multiplication distributes over addition.
Identity and domination: A union empty is A, A intersect U is A, A union U is the whole universe U, and A intersect empty is empty. Empty and U behave like zero and everything.
Complement laws: A union A prime fills the universe U, A intersect A prime is empty since nothing is both in and out, and complementing twice returns A.
The two De Morgan laws, worth memorising cold: complement of A union B is A prime intersect B prime, and complement of A intersect B is A prime union B prime. The operation flips.

And the bridge to every word problem, the two set cardinality formula: n of A union B equals n of A plus n of B minus n of A intersect B. You subtract the overlap because adding the two sizes counts it twice.

segments.text: Let's run all five operations on one concrete example so the definitions become muscle memory.
The universe is one through ten. A is two, four, six, eight, the even numbers up to eight. B is one through five.
Union first, everything in either set: one, two, three, four, five, six, eight. Intersection next, only what's common to both: two and four.
A minus B, in A but not in B, strips out two and four, leaving six and eight. And A prime, the complement, is the universe minus A: one, three, five, seven, nine, ten.
For the symmetric difference we also need B minus A, in B but not in A, which is one, three, five.
Now A triangle B is A minus B, unioned with B minus A, that's six, eight together with one, three, five, giving one, three, five, six, eight, exactly the elements in one set but not the other.
And notice the reminder: A minus B is not B minus A. Difference always reads left to right, source set first, then remove the second.
Here's a simplification where the fast method beats the algebra hands down. Simplify A minus B, unioned with A intersect B.
The speed move is: shade, don't grind. Picture the Venn and let the regions do the work.
A minus B is the 'only A' crescent, the part of A outside B. A intersect B is the lens, the overlap. Now put those two together, the crescent plus the lens, and they fill the entire circle A.
So immediately, A minus B unioned with A intersect B is just A. A five second answer once you visualise the regions.
For the algebraic confirmation, use the identity A minus B equals A intersect B prime.

Then A intersect B prime, unioned with A intersect B, factors as A intersect the quantity B prime union B. But B prime union B is the whole universe U, so this is A intersect U, which is A. The algebra lands exactly where the picture did.
The trap here is students rushing to A union B, over shading into B, or to A intersect B, under shading. The crescent plus lens picture protects you from both.
Intervals are where domain problems in calculus quietly begin, and endpoints are exactly where marks are won or lost. Let's operate on two of them over the reals.
A is the interval from minus two to five, closed at minus two, open at five. B is from one to eight, open at one, closed at eight.

For the intersection, we need numbers in both. The left edge is the larger of the two lower bounds, that's one, and it's open because B excludes it. The right edge is the smaller of the two upper bounds, that's five, open because A excludes it. So the intersection is open one to five.
For the union, numbers in either. The left edge is minus two, closed, coming from A. The right edge is eight, closed, coming from B. So the union is the closed interval minus two to eight.

For A minus B, we want points in A but not in B. B starts just above one, and crucially one is not in B, so one survives in the difference. So A minus B runs from minus two up to and including one, that's the closed interval minus two to one.
Look at the number line. A on top, closed dot at minus two, open dot at five. B below, open dot at one, filled dot at eight. The shaded overlap between one and five is the intersection.

The rule to carry: for intersection, take the tighter bounds and the stricter brackets. For union of overlapping intervals, take the looser bounds. The bracket shape is the inequality, so getting endpoints right is the whole game.
An Advanced style proof. Symmetric difference has two standard definitions, and we prove they describe exactly the same set.
The claim: A union B, minus A intersect B, equals A minus B, unioned with B minus A. The left side removes the overlap from the union, the right side glues together the two crescents.
We element chase. Take any x. x is in the left side exactly when x is in at least one of A and B, and x is not in both of them.
Now read that condition plainly. In at least one, and not in both, is precisely the phrase 'in exactly one of A and B'.
And 'exactly one' splits into two mutually exclusive cases: either x is in A and not in B, or x is in B and not in A.
But those two cases are exactly x in A minus B, or x in B minus A, which together is x in the union of A minus B with B minus A, the right hand side.

Every step was an if and only if, so the two sets have identical elements, and the proof is complete. The insight to keep: symmetric difference is just the everyday phrase 'one or the other, but not both'.
Let's collect the operation traps, the small slips that quietly turn a right method into a wrong answer.
Trap one, treating difference as commutative. A minus B is not B minus A. Always read which set is the source, the one you keep, and which one is being removed.

Trap two, swapping the two De Morgan forms. Complement of a union is the intersection of complements, and complement of an intersection is the union of complements. The operation flips, don't put it back the wrong way.
Trap three, forgetting to fix the universe before taking a complement. A prime is undefined until U is stated, and the answer literally changes with U.
Trap four, endpoint errors in interval operations. For intersection, take the tighter bounds and the stricter brackets. For union of overlapping intervals, take the looser bounds.
Trap five, confusing disjoint with complementary. Disjoint just means the intersection is empty. Complementary means disjoint and their union fills the whole universe. Disjoint alone is weaker.

And the pro tip that saves the most time: for any expression in two sets, draw the four region Venn once and shade. Shading is faster and far less error prone than juggling the laws, and it instantly tells you whether your algebra landed on A, on A union B, or on A intersect B.

We element chase. Take any x. x is in the left side exactly when x is in at least one of A and B, and x is not in both of them.
Now read that condition plainly. In at least one, and not in both, is precisely the phrase 'in exactly one of A and B'.
And 'exactly one' splits into two mutually exclusive cases: either x is in A and not in B, or x is in B and not in A.
But those two cases are exactly x in A minus B, or x in B minus A, which together is x in the union of A minus B with B minus A, the right hand side.

Every step was an if and only if, so the two sets have identical elements, and the proof is complete. The insight to keep: symmetric difference is just the everyday phrase 'one or the other, but not both'.
Let's collect the operation traps, the small slips that quietly turn a right method into a wrong answer.
Trap one, treating difference as commutative. A minus B is not B minus A. Always read which set is the source, the one you keep, and which one is being removed.

Trap two, swapping the two De Morgan forms. Complement of a union is the intersection of complements, and complement of an intersection is the union of complements. The operation flips, don't put it back the wrong way.
Trap three, forgetting to fix the universe before taking a complement. A prime is undefined until U is stated, and the answer literally changes with U.
Trap four, endpoint errors in interval operations. For intersection, take the tighter bounds and the stricter brackets. For union of overlapping intervals, take the looser bounds.
Trap five, confusing disjoint with complementary. Disjoint just means the intersection is empty. Complementary means disjoint and their union fills the whole universe. Disjoint alone is weaker.

And the pro tip that saves the most time: for any expression in two sets, draw the four region Venn once and shade. Shading is faster and far less error prone than juggling the laws, and it instantly tells you whether your algebra landed on A, on A union B, or on A intersect B.

segments.text: This subtopic is one of the highest yield scoring topics in the whole chapter, and it all rests on a single observation about double counting.

Say a coaching batch has seventy students in Physics and fifty in Chemistry. How many take at least one of the two? The tempting answer is one hundred twenty, but that's almost always wrong, because some students take both.

Here's why. When you counted the seventy Physics students you already swept up the both subject students, and when you counted the fifty Chemistry students you counted those same people a second time. Adding double counts the overlap, so to fix it you subtract the overlap once.
That gives the two set formula: n of A union B equals n of A plus n of B minus n of A intersect B. Add the two sizes, remove one copy of the overlap.
As a check, when A and B are disjoint the overlap is zero, and the formula collapses neatly to just n of A plus n of B, exactly what you'd expect when nobody's shared.
Keep the translation dictionary handy: 'or' means union, 'and' means intersection, and the word 'only A' means drop the overlaps and keep A's private part.

One more distinction that examiners love: at least one versus none. Those in none of the sets are the complement of the union, so their count is n of U minus n of the union. At least one is the union, none is everything outside it.
Now scale from two sets to three, say Physics, Chemistry, and Mathematics. Building the count honestly, region by region, forces a beautiful alternating pattern.
Step one, add the three individual sizes. But now every two way overlap has been counted twice, and the central three way overlap, the region inside all three circles, has been counted three times.

Step two, subtract the three pairwise overlaps. This fixes the two way regions, they're now counted once. But watch the centre: it was added three times, then subtracted three times, since it sits inside all three pairwise overlaps, so right now it's counted zero times.
Step three, add the triple overlap back once. Now the centre is counted exactly once too, and everything balances.
So the three set formula is: n of A union B union C equals the sum of the three single sizes, minus the sum of the three pairwise overlaps, plus the triple overlap.

The picture shows all of this: three overlapping circles carve out seven inner regions, only A, only B, only C, the three pairwise slivers, and the central triple overlap, plus the eighth region, none, sitting outside all three.
And notice the signs, plus, minus, plus, include, exclude, include. That alternation is exactly why this rule is called the inclusion exclusion principle.

Here is the full family of counting identities. A quick notation note: the sigma over single sets means n of A plus n of B plus n of C, and the sigma over pairs means the sum of the three pairwise overlaps.
The two set union: n of A union B equals n of A plus n of B minus n of A intersect B.
The three set union: the sum of the singles, minus the sum of the pairwise overlaps, plus the triple overlap. Include, exclude, include.
Exactly one set: the sum of singles, minus twice the sum of pairwise overlaps, plus three times the triple overlap. This strips a person down to living in precisely one circle.

Exactly two sets: the sum of pairwise overlaps, minus three times the triple overlap. Each pairwise overlap includes the all three group once, so summing all three counts the centre three times, and we remove all three copies.

At least two sets: the sum of pairwise overlaps, minus only two times the triple overlap. Here we want the centre counted once, not zero, so we subtract two copies instead of three. That single difference separates exactly two from at least two.

And the two partition identities, the secret weapon when an overlap is unknown. Writing E one, E two, E three for the counts in exactly one, exactly two, and all three regions: the union equals E one plus E two plus E three, and the sum of the single sizes equals E one plus two E two plus three E three, because each person is counted once per set they belong to.

board_events.text: 120 students, Physics & Chemistry
'only P' = P minus the overlap; 'neither' = U minus the union.
Everyone takes at least one service
80 students; tea 60, coffee 35; every student takes ≥ 1 service.
'At least one' ⇒ union = total = 80. This is the whole key.
Decoy instinct: compute $60 + 35 = 95$ and panic that it exceeds 80.
That excess $95 - 80 = 15$ IS the double-counted overlap.
Cricket, Football, Hockey (200 students)
'Exactly two' subtracts 3× the centre; 'at least two' would subtract only 2×.
Fill the centre (20) first, then work outward — every region reads off directly.
Find how many speak all three languages
Union = 150 (all speak ≥ 1); $\sum n = 100+70+55 = 225$; $E_2 = 25$ (exactly two).
25 speak all three. Check: $E_3=25, E_2=25 \Rightarrow E_1=100$; union $=150$ ✓.
When the triple overlap is unknown, the two partition identities finish it — no diagram needed.
Word-problem traps
Forgetting to subtract the overlap. $n(A\cup B)=n(A)+n(B)$ only for disjoint sets.
Confusing 'only A' with 'A'. 'Only' strips out every overlap.
Mis-signing the three-way term: +singles − pairs + triple.
'Exactly two' subtracts 3× the centre; 'at least two' subtracts 2×.
Sanity-check: negative region, or union > n(U), ⇒ data is inconsistent — say so.
PRO-TIP: draw the Venn, fill the centre first, then work outward — read every answer off the regions.

segments.text: A bread and butter board problem. A batch of one hundred twenty students, seventy in Physics, fifty in Chemistry, thirty in both. We want three counts.
Write down the givens cleanly. The universe is one hundred twenty, Physics is seventy, Chemistry is fifty, and the intersection, both subjects, is thirty.
First, at least one of the two subjects, that's the union. By the two set formula, seventy plus fifty minus thirty, which is ninety. Ninety students take at least one subject.
Second, Physics only. That's Physics minus the overlap, seventy minus thirty, which is forty. These are the students in Physics but not Chemistry.
Third, neither subject. That's the universe minus the union, one hundred twenty minus ninety, which is thirty. Thirty students take neither.

The two phrases to read carefully: only P means Physics minus the overlap, and neither means the universe minus the union. Get those two mappings right and the whole family of two set word problems opens up.

A speed trap that turns on reading one phrase correctly. In a hostel of eighty students, sixty subscribe to a tea service and thirty five to a coffee service, and every student takes at least one of the two. How many take both?
The numbers: eighty students total, tea sixty, coffee thirty five, and the crucial condition, every student subscribes to at least one service.
Here's the whole key. Every student takes at least one, which means the union, tea or coffee, equals the total, eighty. That phrase hands you the union for free.

Now rearrange the two set formula to solve for the overlap. n of both equals n of tea plus n of coffee minus n of the union, that's sixty plus thirty five minus eighty, which is fifteen. Fifteen students take both.
The decoy instinct is to compute sixty plus thirty five equals ninety five and then panic, because ninety five exceeds the eighty students in the hostel.

But don't panic, embrace it. That excess, ninety five minus eighty equals fifteen, is exactly the double counted overlap, the people counted in both tea and coffee. So the excess itself is the answer.

A full three set survey. Two hundred students, one hundred play cricket, eighty football, sixty five hockey, with pairwise overlaps forty, thirty, and thirty five, and twenty playing all three. We want at least one, exactly two, and none.

First gather the ingredients. The sum of singles is one hundred plus eighty plus sixty five, which is two hundred forty five. The sum of pairwise overlaps is forty plus thirty plus thirty five, which is one hundred five. And the triple overlap is twenty.
At least one is the union. Include exclude include: two hundred forty five, minus one hundred five, plus twenty, which is one hundred sixty. So one hundred sixty students play at least one sport.

Exactly two uses the sum of pairwise overlaps minus three times the triple. That's one hundred five minus three times twenty, which is one hundred five minus sixty, giving forty five. Forty five students play exactly two sports.
No sport is the universe minus the union: two hundred minus one hundred sixty, which is forty. Forty students play no sport at all.

Notice the key distinction in the exactly two formula: we subtract three times the centre. If the question had asked at least two, we'd subtract only two times the centre, keeping it counted once. That one coefficient is the whole difference.

And the reliable habit: fill the centre, the twenty, first, then work outward through the pairwise and single regions. Once the diagram is labelled, every only, exactly, and at least answer reads straight off it.

An Advanced problem where the unknown is the triple overlap itself, so we reach for the partition identities. In a colony of one hundred fifty residents, everyone speaks at least one of Hindi, English, or Tamil. One hundred speak Hindi, seventy English, fifty five Tamil, and exactly twenty five speak precisely two languages. How many speak all three?

Set up the knowns. Since everyone speaks at least one, the union is one hundred fifty. The sum of the single sizes is one hundred plus seventy plus fifty five, which is two hundred twenty five. And exactly two, which is E two, is twenty five.
Now the first partition identity: the union equals E one plus E two plus E three. So E one plus twenty five plus E three equals one hundred fifty.
The second identity: the sum of the single sizes equals E one plus two E two plus three E three. So E one plus fifty plus three E three equals two hundred twenty five.

Subtract the first equation from the second. The E one cancels, and we get fifty minus twenty five, plus three E three minus E three, equals two hundred twenty five minus one hundred fifty, that is twenty five plus two E three equals seventy five, so E three is twenty five.

So twenty five residents speak all three languages. Quick check: with E three twenty five and E two twenty five, the first identity gives E one equals one hundred, and the union is one hundred plus twenty five plus twenty five, which is one hundred fifty. It all balances.
The lesson: when the three way overlap is the unknown, the two partition identities give you two equations in the unknowns, and pure algebra finishes the job without ever drawing the diagram.
Let's lock down the word problem traps, because this is the highest scoring topic and examiners plant marks in exactly these spots.
Trap one, forgetting to subtract the overlap. n of A union B equals n of A plus n of B is correct only for disjoint sets. With any overlap at all, you must subtract n of A intersect B.
Trap two, confusing only A with A. Only strips out every overlap, plain A keeps them. Before computing, underline the words only, exactly, at least, and neither, they each mean a different region.
Trap three, mis signing the three way term. In the union formula the alternating pattern is plus singles, minus pairs, plus triple. Get the last sign wrong and the whole answer shifts.

Trap four, treating exactly two and at least two as the same. They differ by exactly one copy of the centre: subtract three times the triple overlap for exactly two, but only two times for at least two.

Trap five, not sanity checking against the universe. If a region comes out negative, or the union exceeds n of U, the data is inconsistent, and the correct exam answer is to say the data is impossible, not to force a number.

And the pro tip for every fully specified three set problem: draw the Venn, fill the centre first, then work outward. Once the regions are labelled, every only, exactly, and at least answer reads straight off, no formula recall under pressure, and a negative region instantly exposes bad data.

The two phrases to read carefully: only P means Physics minus the overlap, and neither means the universe minus the union. Get those two mappings right and the whole family of two set word problems opens up.

A speed trap that turns on reading one phrase correctly. In a hostel of eighty students, sixty subscribe to a tea service and thirty five to a coffee service, and every student takes at least one of the two. How many take both?
The numbers: eighty students total, tea sixty, coffee thirty five, and the crucial condition, every student subscribes to at least one service.
Here's the whole key. Every student takes at least one, which means the union, tea or coffee, equals the total, eighty. That phrase hands you the union for free.

Now rearrange the two set formula to solve for the overlap. n of both equals n of tea plus n of coffee minus n of the union, that's sixty plus thirty five minus eighty, which is fifteen. Fifteen students take both.
The decoy instinct is to compute sixty plus thirty five equals ninety five and then panic, because ninety five exceeds the eighty students in the hostel.

But don't panic, embrace it. That excess, ninety five minus eighty equals fifteen, is exactly the double counted overlap, the people counted in both tea and coffee. So the excess itself is the answer.

A full three set survey. Two hundred students, one hundred play cricket, eighty football, sixty five hockey, with pairwise overlaps forty, thirty, and thirty five, and twenty playing all three. We want at least one, exactly two, and none.

First gather the ingredients. The sum of singles is one hundred plus eighty plus sixty five, which is two hundred forty five. The sum of pairwise overlaps is forty plus thirty plus thirty five, which is one hundred five. And the triple overlap is twenty.
At least one is the union. Include exclude include: two hundred forty five, minus one hundred five, plus twenty, which is one hundred sixty. So one hundred sixty students play at least one sport.

Exactly two uses the sum of pairwise overlaps minus three times the triple. That's one hundred five minus three times twenty, which is one hundred five minus sixty, giving forty five. Forty five students play exactly two sports.
No sport is the universe minus the union: two hundred minus one hundred sixty, which is forty. Forty students play no sport at all.

Notice the key distinction in the exactly two formula: we subtract three times the centre. If the question had asked at least two, we'd subtract only two times the centre, keeping it counted once. That one coefficient is the whole difference.

And the reliable habit: fill the centre, the twenty, first, then work outward through the pairwise and single regions. Once the diagram is labelled, every only, exactly, and at least answer reads straight off it.

An Advanced problem where the unknown is the triple overlap itself, so we reach for the partition identities. In a colony of one hundred fifty residents, everyone speaks at least one of Hindi, English, or Tamil. One hundred speak Hindi, seventy English, fifty five Tamil, and exactly twenty five speak precisely two languages. How many speak all three?

Set up the knowns. Since everyone speaks at least one, the union is one hundred fifty. The sum of the single sizes is one hundred plus seventy plus fifty five, which is two hundred twenty five. And exactly two, which is E two, is twenty five.
Now the first partition identity: the union equals E one plus E two plus E three. So E one plus twenty five plus E three equals one hundred fifty.
The second identity: the sum of the single sizes equals E one plus two E two plus three E three. So E one plus fifty plus three E three equals two hundred twenty five.

Subtract the first equation from the second. The E one cancels, and we get fifty minus twenty five, plus three E three minus E three, equals two hundred twenty five minus one hundred fifty, that is twenty five plus two E three equals seventy five, so E three is twenty five.

So twenty five residents speak all three languages. Quick check: with E three twenty five and E two twenty five, the first identity gives E one equals one hundred, and the union is one hundred plus twenty five plus twenty five, which is one hundred fifty. It all balances.
The lesson: when the three way overlap is the unknown, the two partition identities give you two equations in the unknowns, and pure algebra finishes the job without ever drawing the diagram.
Let's lock down the word problem traps, because this is the highest scoring topic and examiners plant marks in exactly these spots.
Trap one, forgetting to subtract the overlap. n of A union B equals n of A plus n of B is correct only for disjoint sets. With any overlap at all, you must subtract n of A intersect B.
Trap two, confusing only A with A. Only strips out every overlap, plain A keeps them. Before computing, underline the words only, exactly, at least, and neither, they each mean a different region.
Trap three, mis signing the three way term. In the union formula the alternating pattern is plus singles, minus pairs, plus triple. Get the last sign wrong and the whole answer shifts.

Trap four, treating exactly two and at least two as the same. They differ by exactly one copy of the centre: subtract three times the triple overlap for exactly two, but only two times for at least two.

Trap five, not sanity checking against the universe. If a region comes out negative, or the union exceeds n of U, the data is inconsistent, and the correct exam answer is to say the data is impossible, not to force a number.

And the pro tip for every fully specified three set problem: draw the Venn, fill the centre first, then work outward. Once the regions are labelled, every only, exactly, and at least answer reads straight off, no formula recall under pressure, and a negative region instantly exposes bad data.
